C001.name: Differential programming
C001.definition: Differential programming is a programming paradigm where parts of the program are parameterized. This allows gradient-based optimization to tune those parameters to optimize the program or find a local optimum.

C002.name: Pointwise non-linearity
C002.definition: Pointwise non-linearity is a type of non-linearity where the function is applied to each component of the output vector individually. These non-linearities are usually applied element-wise.

C003.name: Generative model
C003.definition: Generative model is a type of model used to create new content, such as text or images, based on learned patterns. These models can be text-based or image-based.

C004.name: Transfer learning
C004.definition: Transfer learning is the technique of reusing components from a previously trained model. This allows knowledge learned for one task, such as categorizing animals, to be applied to a different task, like satellite imagery.

C005.name: Deep learning
C005.definition: Deep learning is a field of study interested in modeling complex phenomena in the real world. It is presented as a possible solution for tackling the difficulty of modeling these complex systems.

C006.name: Complex phenomena
C006.definition: Complex phenomena are real-world subjects that students interact with daily, such as natural language, images, videos, DNA, ecosystems, and climate change. These phenomena are difficult to model using traditional methods.

C007.name: Artificial Intelligence
C007.definition: AI is a field of study whose history the instructor will briefly go over. It is the broader domain within which deep learning operates.

C008.name: Perceptron
C008.definition: Perceptron is the first neural network, which was designed to recognize or categorize images. This basic unit forms the building block for most of the deep learning used today.

C009.name: Backpropagation
C009.definition: Backpropagation is a fundamental concept that enables multilayer perceptrons to be reasonably trained. This concept allows a gradient to be propagated through multiple layers of perceptrons.

C010.name: Multilayer perceptron
C010.definition: Multilayer perceptron is a structure consisting of multiple perceptrons stacked on top of each other. This structure allows the network to solve categorization problems that are not separable from a linear classifier.

C011.name: Convolutional neural network
C011.definition: Convolutional neural network (CNN) is a network architecture where earlier layers produce low-level representations, while later layers combine these into more complex representations.

C012.name: ImageNet
C012.definition: ImageNet is a very large-scale dataset of its kind. This dataset was a vital component that allowed machine learning to begin working effectively.

C013.name: Non-linearity
C013.definition: Non-linearity is the function applied between layers that allows a network to model complex, non-straight relationships. Without this non-linearity, stacking multiple linear layers simply results in a single linear combination.

C014.name: Modular reuse
C014.definition: Modular reuse is the concept within an open source community where trained weights from one architecture can be taken and used as a module within a larger system. This larger system may incorporate many different components pulled from various sources.

C015.name: Gradient descent
C015.definition: Gradient descent is the idea of optimizing a cost function by finding a minimum over the training data. This minimum is a set of parameters where the loss is minimized for all data points, aiming to find the optimal set of model parameters.

C016.name: Parameter
C016.definition: Parameters of a model are all the different layers of weights and biases that the model uses. These parameters are the values that the model adjusts during the learning process.

C017.name: Linear layer
C017.definition: Linear layer is a building block in neural networks where a component of the output representation is calculated as a sum over inputs multiplied by corresponding weights. This calculation can also incorporate a bias term.

C018.name: Bias term
C018.definition: Bias term is a component added to the calculation that does not take in any of the input components. It serves as a constant offset in the linear combination.

C019.name: Rectified linear unit
C019.definition: Rectified linear unit (ReLU) is a pointwise non-linearity defined as the maximum of zero and the input value $z$. This function is super efficient to implement and is widely used in current models.

C020.name: Representational power
C020.definition: Representational power is the theoretical ability of a model to map and represent complex functions. With two or more layers and non-linearity, a deep network can theoretically represent any function.

C021.name: Capacity
C021.definition: Capacity refers to the amount of complexity or number of dimensions a model can handle. Given sufficient capacity, a model can theoretically approximate any function.

C022.name: Deep network
C022.definition: Deep network is a type of neural network that represents data in a more compact way, allowing it to encode knowledge efficiently. This representation is considered an improvement over previous methods like lookup tables.

C023.name: Shallow network
C023.definition: Shallow network is a network structure that, if not sufficiently wide, may only be able to efficiently compute simple tasks, such as finding edges. In contrast, a deep network can efficiently compute much harder tasks.

C024.name: Overparameterized
C024.definition: Overparameterized describes a new paradigm in deep learning, replacing the classical concepts of underfitting and overfitting. This term refers to models that possess a very large number of parameters.

C025.name: Generalize
C025.definition: Generalize is the ability of a model to learn rules that apply broadly, rather than merely memorizing the training data. This allows the model to perform well on data that it has not seen before.

C026.name: Overfitting
C026.definition: Overfitting is the phenomenon where a model learns patterns from the training data so perfectly that it generalizes poorly to new, unseen data. This occurs when the model is too complex, resulting in a 'spiky' or 'peaky' function that fits the training points exactly.

C027.name: Cross-entropy loss
C027.definition: Cross-entropy loss is a function used to measure the distance between the distribution the model predicts and the actual distribution of the input. It forces the network to maximize the probability of the training data, thereby ensuring the output is a reasonable probability model of the object.

C028.name: One hot encoding
C028.definition: One hot encoding is a vector representation used for the ground truth label, where every element is zero except for the correct class, which is marked with a one.

C029.name: Tensor
C029.definition: A tensor is a multi-dimensional matrix that serves as the mathematical representation of the input data and the layers within the model. Essentially, everything in the deep learning model is represented as a tensor.

C030.name: Representation learning
C030.definition: Representation learning is the process of structuring data so that the network can learn concepts. This learning is studied through methods such as reconstruction and similarity.

C031.name: Neural network
C031.definition: Neural network is a structure consisting of a chain of different blocks or layers. Each of these layers has associated parameters that are used during the training process.

C032.name: Loss
C032.definition: Loss is a function used at the end of the network to calculate the cost. This cost is then used when thinking about the learning process.

C033.name: Optimal set of theta
C033.definition: Optimal set of theta is the specific set of parameters that minimizes the loss function. This minimization must occur across all of the available data set.

C034.name: Cost function
C034.definition: Cost function is a measure that quantifies the total loss across all data points in the training data set, which gradient descent seeks to minimize.

C035.name: Gradient
C035.definition: Gradient is a mathematical measure that indicates the direction of maximal change for a parameter set, which is used in optimization algorithms.

C036.name: Learning rate (eta)
C036.definition: Learning rate (eta) is a defined value that determines how far the parameters will step in the direction of the gradient during each iteration.

C037.name: Loss landscape
C037.definition: Loss landscape is the surface that represents the cost function, and it is where the optimization process begins and moves to find a minimum.

C038.name: Global minimum
C038.definition: Global minimum is the single lowest point in the entire loss landscape, representing the optimal solution that minimizes the loss function across all possible parameter settings.

C039.name: Stochastic gradient descent
C039.definition: Stochastic gradient descent is an optimization method that approximates the total gradient by calculating it over a small subset of the data. This approach is used because calculating the gradient over the entire dataset is often computationally intractable.

C040.name: Batch
C040.definition: A batch is a subset of the data that is used to compute the gradient at any given point during the training process. The size of the batch determines how many examples are used before the parameters are updated.

C041.name: Overall loss function
C041.definition: The overall loss function is the total measure of error that the model attempts to minimize. This function is typically calculated as a sum of the individual losses across every single example in the training data.

C042.name: Implicit regularizer
C042.definition: An implicit regularizer is a property of stochastic gradient descent where the inherent noise in the gradient calculation helps stabilize the training process. This noise can assist the model in finding a better solution.

C043.name: Local minima
C043.definition: Local minima is a point in the loss landscape where the function value is lower than all surrounding points, but this point is not necessarily the lowest possible point overall.

C044.name: Momentum
C044.definition: Momentum is a technique in gradient descent that biases gradient steps to continue in the direction of previous updates. This gives the optimization process momentum based on its past direction of movement.

C045.name: Hyperparameter
C045.definition: Hyperparameter is a value, such as alpha, that determines the strength of momentum. This strength is set externally and influences how the optimization process behaves.

C046.name: Adam optimizer (Adam)
C046.definition: Adam optimizer (Adam) is a popular example of a type of momentum used within gradient descent. This optimizer is commonly used in deep learning applications.

C047.name: Differentiable
C047.definition: Differentiable describes a function that possesses a derivative at every point, which is a mathematical property required for calculating slopes and performing optimization.

C048.name: Exploding gradients
C048.definition: Exploding gradient occurs when the gradient increases toward infinity as the minimizer is approached. This results in highly unstable updates, making it difficult to actually hit the minimum.

C049.name: Vanishing gradient
C049.definition: Vanishing gradient is a condition where the gradient becomes extremely small as the minimum is approached, causing the training progress to be very slow. This slow progress can be dominated by noise in the training batches.

C050.name: Multiple local minima
C050.definition: Multiple local minima refers to a loss landscape that is not guaranteed to be convex, meaning it may contain several low-loss regions. When this occurs, the initial model parameters greatly influence which minimum the optimization process finds.

C051.name: Convexity
C051.definition: Convexity is a property of a function, such as a loss landscape, that allows for the assumption of a single minimum. When a function is convex, all gradients point toward that single minimum.

C052.name: Evolution strategy
C052.definition: Evolution strategy is a gradient-like method that finds locally loss-minimizing directions in parameter space. It achieves this by sampling small perturbations around existing parameter values and moving toward perturbations that achieve lower loss.

C053.name: Gradient clipping
C053.definition: Gradient clipping is a mechanism used to help manage peakiness or pointiness in a loss function. It works by scaling back the gradient if it exceeds a predefined large value, essentially placing a clipping filter on the gradient.

C054.name: Gaussian error linear unit
C054.definition: Gaussian error linear unit (GeLU) is a non-linearity that takes the parameters multiplied by the cumulative distribution function for the Gaussian distribution. This function is everywhere continuous, everywhere differentiable, and everywhere smooth.

C055.name: Loss function
C055.definition: Loss function is a function used in training that measures the difference between the predicted output and the actual target. Loss functions can sometimes be set up to have negative values.

C056.name: Computation graph
C056.definition: Computation graph is a graph of different functional transformations where each transformation is represented as a node. Stringing these nodes together allows for the performance of useful computation.

C057.name: Directed acyclic graph
C057.definition: Directed acyclic graph is a graph where information flows only in one direction along any given edge, and the graph contains no loops or cycles.

C058.name: Forward pass
C058.definition: Forward pass is the process of sending data forward through the network. This involves computing the outputs and calculating the overall loss.

C059.name: Cost
C059.definition: Cost is the overall calculation of the loss across all of the data. Cost is also a mechanism used to evaluate the optimality of the model.

C060.name: Jacobian formulation
C060.definition: The Jacobian formulation is a method used to calculate the partial derivative when the output is a vector and the input is a vector. This formulation results in a matrix whose size is determined by the size of the output by the size of the input.

C061.name: Partial derivative
C061.definition: A partial derivative is the rate of change of a function with respect to one specific variable while holding all other variables constant. When the input is a matrix and the output is a scalar, the resulting derivative is also a matrix.

C062.name: Transposed
C062.definition: Transposed refers to the operation of flipping the rows and columns of a matrix. This operation changes the dimensions of the matrix, which is noted when taking certain derivatives.

C063.name: Chain rule
C063.definition: The chain rule is a method used to find the derivative of a composite function, where one function is nested inside another. It involves multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function.

C064.name: Backwards pass
C064.definition: Backward pass is the iterative computation of loss derivatives, moving from the top layer down to the input. This process determines how much each parameter contributed to the overall loss.

C065.name: Layer output gradient (L)
C065.definition: Layer output gradient (L) is a matrix that tracks the gradient of the layer outputs with regard to the layer inputs. This matrix indicates which way the parameters need to change to move in the maximal direction of optimization.

C066.name: Cost gradient (g)
C066.definition: Cost gradient (g) is a row vector representing the gradient of the cost with respect to the activations. This vector essentially states the partial derivative of the cost with respect to the input of that layer.

C067.name: Merging
C067.definition: Merging is an operation that combines functional components to move forward through a directed-acyclic graph. When propagating a gradient back through a merge, one must track the gradient with respect to the correct input variables.

C068.name: Branching
C068.definition: Branching is the process of splitting up or duplicating information within a network. When propagating a gradient back through a branch, the gradients from both paths are summed and sent back through the input.

C069.name: Parameter sharing
C069.definition: Parameter sharing occurs when the parameters are reused across different components of a network, rather than having separate parameters for each component. This allows the network to reuse parameters, such as those pre-trained on ImageNet, in multiple parts of the network.

C070.name: Software 2.0
C070.definition: Software 2.0 is a concept where the software defines a space of possible systems, and the goal is to optimize within that space to build the specific system needed to solve a problem.

C071.name: Feature engineering
C071.definition: Feature engineering is a process where humans build explicit constraints into how the data might be processed before it is fed into a simple neural network.

C072.name: Optimizing inputs
C072.definition: Optimizing inputs involves considering how the cost changes by modifying the input data while keeping the network's parameters fixed. This approach allows for changes to the input, such as changing input pixels.

C073.name: Embedding
C073.definition: Embedding is a mapping that transforms a high-dimensional or complex input, such as an image, into a low-dimensional representation. Embedding is essentially the use of a pre-trained neural network to provide a low-rank representation of the input data.

C074.name: Attention block
C074.definition: Attention block is a component generally defined for a transformer that includes projections into a shared space. This block also includes a projection out into the space where the information is utilized.

C075.name: Universal function approximator
C075.definition: Universal function approximator is a property of a model, meaning that the model can theoretically fit any function, making it a powerful tool for solving complex problems.

C076.name: Approximation
C076.definition: Approximation is the process of representing a function by summing up a collection of indicator functions. The height of each rectangle in this sum is determined by a coefficient, $\alpha_i$.

C077.name: Weierstrass' function
C077.definition: Weierstrass' function is a classic mathematical function that is everywhere continuous but nowhere differentiable. This characteristic makes it a prime example of a pathological function.

C078.name: Pathological function
C078.definition: A pathological function is a function that exhibits unusual or counter-intuitive mathematical properties. Weierstrass' function serves as a classic example of this type of function.

C079.name: Fractal function
C079.definition: A fractal function is a function that is defined recursively and is self-similar. This means that if any part of the function is magnified, it resembles the entire function.

C080.name: Approximation problem
C080.definition: The approximation problem asks whether a neural network within a specified family can fit a function from a target family of curves to a small error. This formalizes the question of whether a neural network can represent a given set of functions.

C081.name: L-infinity error
C081.definition: The L-infinity error is a measure of discrepancy between two functions, calculated as the maximum absolute difference between the two functions across all inputs. This represents the largest discrepancy between the two functions anywhere on the input space.

C082.name: L-Lipschitz function
C082.definition: L-Lipschitz function is a type of function that has bounded derivatives. This property restricts the rate at which the function can change across its domain.

C083.name: Norm
C083.definition: A norm is a mathematical function used to measure the size or length of a vector. It allows us to quantify how large a vector is.

C084.name: RMS norm
C084.definition: The RMS norm is a specific type of vector norm defined as the square root of (1/d) times the sum of the coordinates squared. This norm is used to measure the size of a vector.

C085.name: Euclidean norm
C085.definition: The Euclidean norm is a specific vector norm that measures the size of a vector. It is characterized as a dimensional object.

C086.name: Hypercube
C086.definition: A hypercube is a geometric shape used to constrain data, allowing for arbitrary sizes in different dimensions, which is sometimes referred to as a hypercuboid.

C087.name: Three-layer ReLU network
C087.definition: Three-layer ReLU network is a specific type of neural network structure characterized by having three weight matrices. This structure includes two value functions that follow the first and second weight matrices.

C088.name: Integral notion of error
C088.definition: Integral notion of error is a measure of approximation quality that sums up all the absolute differences between the neural network's output and the target function g. This summation is performed across all the little pieces of the domain.

C089.name: Number of units
C089.definition: Number of units refers to the total count of neurons within the ReLU Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). This count includes all neurons across the network's layers.

C090.name: Lipschitz constant
C090.definition: The Lipschitz constant is a scaling number that constrains the function, and the complexity of the approximation depends on this constant raised to the power of the dimension.

C091.name: Hyperrectangle
C091.definition: Hyperrectangle is the multidimensional generalization of a rectangle, which is used to partition the input space when dealing with multiple inputs.

C092.name: Two-layer ReLU network
C092.definition: A two-layer ReLU network is a specific neural network architecture that the strategy aims to show can approximate a hyperrectangle.

C093.name: Rectangle
C093.definition: A rectangle is a basic building block used in the initial step of the proof strategy to approximate a function in one dimension.

C094.name: Indicator
C094.definition: Indicator is a function that returns 1 if the input value falls within a specific interval, and 0 otherwise. Indicator functions are used as building blocks to construct the function approximation.

C095.name: Approximation error
C095.definition: Approximation error is the measure of the difference or 'gap' between the original function and its approximation. This error can be bounded based on the number of strips and the Lipschitz constant.

C096.name: L1 error
C096.definition: L1 error is the specific measure used to quantify the total error of the function approximation. This error corresponds to the sum of the absolute differences between the function and its approximation.

C097.name: Error cap
C097.definition: Error cap is the height of the hyperrectangle where it differs from the surface G, which is used to measure the maximum possible height of the hyperrectangle.

C098.name: Function g
C098.definition: Function g is a function that takes multiple inputs and produces a single output, which is conceptualized as a surface.

C099.name: Surface
C099.definition: Surface is the representation of a function with multiple inputs and one output, which is generalized from a 2D case.

C100.name: Hyperrectangle function
C100.definition: Hyperrectangle function is a function that represents a geometric shape, specifically a hyperrectangle, in a high-dimensional space. This function is used in the context of approximation theory as a basis function.

C101.name: Indicator function
C101.definition: Indicator function is a function that returns a value of 1 if the input lies within a specific interval or region, and 0 otherwise. This function is used to symbolically represent a geometric shape in a weighted sum.

C102.name: Generalization performance
C102.definition: Generalization performance refers to how well a trained model performs on new, unseen data. Poor generalization performance indicates that the model performs well on training data but fails when applied to real-world data.

C103.name: Stone-Weierstrass theorem
C103.definition: Stone-Weierstrass theorem is a classic result that demonstrates how polynomials can be used to approximate any continuous function. This theorem is related to the mathematical branch of approximation theory.

C104.name: Taylor's expansion
C104.definition: Taylor's expansion is a valid mathematical method for approximating a function by fitting a Taylor series up to a certain degree. This method is similar to the Weierstrass concept of using polynomials to fit a continuous function.

C105.name: Neural net
C105.definition: Neural net is a structure used in deep learning that is fundamentally different from methods like Taylor series when approximating functions. The way a neural net operates is distinct from traditional mathematical approximation techniques.

C106.name: Barron's theorem
C106.definition: Barron's theorem is a classic result that utilizes the Fourier representation of the function being fitted. This theorem provides a specific mathematical basis for function approximation.

C107.name: Width
C107.definition: Width is a structural parameter of a network that must be at least equal to the input space dimension to approximate any function. This establishes a minimum required width for the network.

C108.name: Depth
C108.definition: Depth refers to the number of layers in a neural network. The segment discusses how small depth networks can sometimes be sufficient to fit any function.

C109.name: Depth separation result
C109.definition: A depth separation result is a finding that deeper networks can fit certain kinds of functions using significantly fewer neurons. This efficiency is attributed to the compositionality inherent in deeper network architectures.

C110.name: Piecewise linear function
C110.definition: A piecewise linear function is a function that, when broken into segments, consists of segments that are linear. These linear segments are then stitched together to form the complete function.

C111.name: Kink
C111.definition: A kink is a point in a function where there is a discontinuity in the derivative. It represents a location where the derivative of the function suddenly changes.

C112.name: Piecewise linear
C112.definition: Piecewise linear refers to a function that maintains its piecewise linear property when combined through addition, scalar multiplication, or composition. This property allows the construction of complex functions from simpler linear components.

C113.name: ReLU network
C113.definition: A ReLU network is a neural network structure built using ReLU functions, which ensures that the overall function represented by the network is piecewise linear. The network's complexity is therefore tied to the number of linear segments it contains.

C114.name: Layer
C114.definition: A layer is a component within a deep ReLU network that transforms the function from the previous layer. This transformation involves applying the ReLU function to the result of multiplying the previous function by a weight matrix and adding a bias.

C115.name: Upper bound
C115.definition: An upper bound is a mathematical limit that describes the maximum possible growth rate of a property, such as the number of kinks. The segment shows that this bound grows polynomially in width but exponentially in depth.

C116.name: Loss
C116.definition: Loss is the test loss, which is the metric used to measure how well the model is performing. The loss must eventually go to zero.

C117.name: Confounders
C117.definition: Confounders are a concept that the instructor wants to draw attention to regarding the experimental findings.

C118.name: Confounding issue
C118.definition: A confounding issue is an aspect of the training process that is not fully understood but still has a bearing on the results of an experiment. This issue makes it difficult to isolate the true cause of observed changes in network performance.

C119.name: Very wide shallow neural net
C119.definition: A very wide shallow neural net is a three-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that is wide enough to be capable of fitting any function within a broad class of functions. This type of network demonstrates the capacity to approximate a wide range of functions.

C120.name: Sequential structure
C120.definition: Sequential structure refers to data where the elements are inherently ordered in a specific sequence, such as a waveform.

C121.name: Two-dimensional structure
C121.definition: Two-dimensional structure refers to data that possesses inherent spatial dimensions, such as an image.

C122.name: Universal approximator
C122.definition: Universal approximator is a property of a model that allows it to approximate any mathematical function.

C123.name: Inductive biases
C123.definition: Inductive biases are the inherent assumptions baked into a model, which dictate what structure or intuition the model assumes about the function it is trying to learn.

C124.name: Dense layer
C124.definition: Dense layer, also known as a fully connected layer, is a type of layer where the weights can be applied in parallel across a very large batch of data, independently per data point.

C125.name: Convolutional layers
C125.definition: Convolutional layers are a specific mechanism that can be built into an architecture, which works particularly well for grid data.

C126.name: Mapping
C126.definition: Mapping is the function that describes all possible relationships from an input set (X) to an output set (Y). This set represents all possible functions that could solve the problem.

C127.name: Hypothesis space
C127.definition: Hypothesis space is a defined subset of all possible models, which adds structure to the model itself. This space shines a spotlight on a specific portion of the overall space of all possible models.

C128.name: Architectures
C128.definition: Architectures are structures that enable a model to generalize outside of the training distribution. A good architecture must be able to represent the true function of the data while remaining otherwise minimal.

C129.name: Sinusoidal activation space
C129.definition: Sinusoidal activation space is a model type that utilizes sinusoidal activations. This type of activation space is particularly efficient for fitting image data.

C130.name: Generalization out of distribution
C130.definition: Generalization out of distribution refers to the model's ability to perform well on data that is different from the data used during training. Poor generalization means the model performs badly when tested on new, unseen data.

C131.name: Semantic segmentation
C131.definition: Semantic segmentation is an image-to-image task where the output space has a spatial structure, meaning it assigns meaning to every part of the image rather than just providing a single category.

C132.name: Patch
C132.definition: Patch is a small piece of the image that is subdivided and used as input for a classifier. Using patches allows the model to classify local regions of the image.

C133.name: Translation invariant
C133.definition: Translation invariant is a property achieved by building constraints into the system, meaning the model's function remains consistent even when the input is shifted. This allows the model to generalize across different input locations.

C134.name: Equivariant mapping
C134.definition: Equivariant mapping is a type of mapping where applying a translation to the input results in a corresponding translation of the function's output. This property ensures that the model maintains a consistent relationship between input and output under spatial shifts.

C135.name: Convolution
C135.definition: Convolution is a linear, shift-invariant transformation applied to grid-structured input data. Essentially, convolution is a method used in signal processing to perform filtering.

C136.name: Convolutional kernel
C136.definition: Convolutional kernel is a set of linear weights (W) that can be applied to an entire image. This kernel functions as the specific set of weights used when performing convolution.

C137.name: Filter
C137.definition: Filter is a single component used in crafting a convolutional layer. Filters are responsible for performing the specific computations that extract features from the input data.

C138.name: Fully connected layer
C138.definition: A fully connected layer is a type of network where all of the outputs depend on all of the inputs. This design can become computationally expensive when the input size is very large.

C139.name: Toeplitz matrix
C139.definition: A Toeplitz matrix is a specific form of matrix that arises when the weight matrix is sparse and the values are the same along the entire diagonal. This structure is characteristic of certain convolutional layers.

C140.name: Equivariant to translation
C140.definition: Equivariant to translation is a built-in hypothesis of convolutional layers. This property means that if the input image is shifted, the resulting output will also shift by the same amount.

C141.name: Receptive field
C141.definition: Receptive field is the area of the input image that influences a specific output unit. This field increases as more layers are added to the model's depth.

C142.name: Patch processing
C142.definition: Patch processing is the ability of convolutional layers to process small, localized sections of the input data. This capability builds in explicit parallelism into the computation.

C143.name: Filter bank
C143.definition: Filter bank is a set of different output convolutions that are learned in parallel when a convolutional layer needs to produce multiple channels of output. Instead of learning a single linear layer, the filter bank allows the network to build multiple independent output dimensions from the same data

C144.name: Multi-channel inputs
C144.definition: Multi-channel inputs refer to data that has depth, such as color images (like RGB), meaning the input is not just a spatial extent but a tensor with multiple channels. When performing convolution on these inputs, a different set of weights is learned for each input channel.

C145.name: Feature channel
C145.definition: Feature channel is one of the dimensions of the output of a convolutional layer, representing a specific feature map generated by a filter. The number of feature channels corresponds to the number of filters used in the convolutional layer.

C146.name: Spatial extent
C146.definition: Spatial extent refers to the dimensions of the filter, such as 3 by 3. This is the convention used when discussing filter size, focusing only on the spatial dimensions rather than the channel dimensions.

C147.name: Feature map
C147.definition: Feature map is an image that serves as a structural representation of the input data. It has height and width and is generated by applying a filter to the input.

C148.name: Feature bank
C148.definition: Feature bank is the collection of learned output channels that a convolutional layer produces. This bank shows what different filters activate when the input image is processed.

C149.name: Feature collapse
C149.definition: Feature collapse is a phenomenon where some features are ignored by the model. This can occur depending on the data, architecture, and optimization process.

C150.name: Pooling
C150.definition: Pooling is a function applied to a local patch that is essentially the same as running a convolutional layer without learning weights. This function uses predefined operations, such as the maximum or average function, to constrain the layer.

C151.name: Downsampling
C151.definition: Downsampling is a method used in neural networks, particularly for classification, where the high-dimensional input structure is intentionally reduced. This is done when the network does not require the full dimensional structure at every layer.

C152.name: Strided operation
C152.definition: Strided operation is a method that combines convolution or pooling with downsampling into a single element. It achieves this by increasing the stride of the filter, causing it to move further than a single pixel at each step.

C153.name: Dilated filter
C153.definition: Dilated filter is a type of filter where certain values are set to zero, which is baked into the model. This configuration allows the filter to capture information from a larger spatial context or extent while using fewer parameters.

C154.name: Neural architecture search
C154.definition: Neural architecture search is a field of research that specifically attempts to optimize over the vast space of possible architectures. This process aims to find the best possible solution for a given task.

C155.name: Feature activations
C155.definition: Feature activations are the outputs of a layer that represent complex information collected from the input image. These activations can become more semantically meaningful as they pass through multiple layers of the network.

C156.name: Encoder-decoder architecture
C156.definition: Encoder-decoder architecture is a structure that processes an input by first using convolution and downsampling to create a low-dimensional representation, and then uses convolution and upsampling to reconstruct the output.

C157.name: U-net
C157.definition: U-net is an architecture designed to bridge the gap between preserving high-resolution structure and maintaining computational efficiency, making it suitable for image-to-image tasks.

C158.name: Skip connection
C158.definition: Skip connection is a connection across different parts of an architecture that allows information to bypass intermediate layers and pass directly toward the output. This mechanism ensures the model does not have to force fine-grained spatial detail into a low-rank embedding.

C159.name: ResNet architecture
C159.definition: ResNet architecture is a deep learning model that utilizes a skipped connection in every single layer. This design allows the model to implicitly learn the optimal depth required for a specific task.

C160.name: Residual connection
C160.definition: Residual connection is a specific type of connection where the output of a layer is calculated by adding the layer's function output to the input dimension itself. This connection assumes that the output and the residual connection are the same size.

C161.name: Convolutions in time
C161.definition: Convolutions in time involve performing convolutions over a temporal dimension, allowing the model to build representations using time as one of the dimensions.

C162.name: 3D convolutions
C162.definition: 3D convolutions are a type of convolution that operates over both spatial dimensions and a temporal dimension, resulting in a lower dimensional representation.

C163.name: Shift invariant in time
C163.definition: Shift invariant in time is a property where the model's output remains the same regardless of when an event occurs within the temporal sequence.

C164.name: Positional encoding
C164.definition: Positional encoding is a method of adding location information to the input of convolutional filters. Positional encoding is constructed separately and added to the input signal, allowing the network to incorporate positional data into the convolution.

C165.name: Neural field
C165.definition: Neural field is a field that is parameterized fully or in part by a neural network. Neural field represents a varying physical quantity across both spatial and temporal coordinates.

C166.name: Neural Radiance Field
C166.definition: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) is a popular architecture that applies a convolutional network to a map. NeRF takes a five-dimensional coordinate grid, which includes position and camera direction, as input and outputs color and volumetric density.

C167.name: Strided convolution
C167.definition: Strided convolution is a method that explicitly performs both pooling and downsampling simultaneously. This technique combines two operations into a single convolutional layer.

C168.name: Fast and slow
C168.definition: Fast and slow is a two-pronged model approach where one model handles motion using low-dimensional subsampling. A secondary channel simultaneously models fine-grained semantic details using high-resolution inputs.

C169.name: Graph neural network
C169.definition: Graph neural network is an architecture that generalizes convolutional networks and is designed to be applied to specific types of problems. Graph neural networks are a type of architecture that is being introduced in this lecture.

C170.name: Message-passing algorithm
C170.definition: Message-passing algorithm is the primary method by which graph neural networks operate. This algorithm functions as a standard neural network that includes both a forward pass and a backward pass.

C171.name: Approximation power
C171.definition: Approximation power refers to the capacity of a neural network to represent different types of functions. It also addresses the degree to which an architecture is universal.

C172.name: Constraints
C172.definition: Constraints are limitations added to a function approximator to rule out certain types of functions. This design choice allows the system to fit data only in specific, desired ways.

C173.name: Transformer
C173.definition: Transformer is the name given to a system where the aggregation operator is attention. This system utilizes attention to aggregate information across the graph structure.

C174.name: Graph nets
C174.definition: Graph nets are a type of network that uses attention as its aggregation operator. This structure allows the network to process information across a graph using attention-based aggregation.

C175.name: Node classification problem
C175.definition: Node classification problem is a task where a question is asked about a specific node within a graph. This involves predicting a property or category for that individual node, such as whether a person likes a certain type of music.

C176.name: Graph prediction problem
C176.definition: Graph prediction problem involves asking a question about the entire graph structure, such as a molecule. This type of problem aims to predict properties based on the overall arrangement of atoms and bonds.

C177.name: Probabilistic graphical model
C177.definition: Probabilistic graphical model is a classical idea for representing probability distributions using a graph structure. Graph nets are appropriate for representing things like these distributions.

C178.name: Discrete optimization
C178.definition: Discrete optimization is a type of problem where decision variables are being optimized. The goal is to find a setting for these variables that satisfies a system of constraints.

C179.name: Node embedding
C179.definition: Node embedding is a vector that is learned specifically for each individual node within a graph. This vector provides information of interest about that particular node.

C180.name: Graph embedding
C180.definition: Graph embedding is a single vector that is learned to represent the entire graph. This vector allows for questions to be asked about the properties of the whole graph.

C181.name: Attribute vector
C181.definition: Attribute vector is the observed data associated with a single node in the graph. This vector provides specific information about that node.

C182.name: Adjacency matrix
C182.definition: Adjacency matrix is a representation used to describe the edges between nodes in a graph. This matrix serves as an additional input to the graph neural network.

C183.name: Permutation invariance
C183.definition: Permutation-invariant describes a function whose output remains the same even if the input items are reordered. This property ensures that the order in which neighbors are indexed does not affect the resulting message.

C184.name: Permutation equivariance
C184.definition: Permutation equivariance is a property where if the input data is permuted (reindexed), the output predictions are permuted in the exact same way. This ensures that shuffling the nodes results in a corresponding shuffle of the predictions.

C185.name: Permutation matrix
C185.definition: Permutation matrix is a matrix used to reorder the rows and columns of another matrix. Applying this matrix changes the indexing of the nodes without changing the underlying structure of the graph.

C186.name: Local operation
C186.definition: Local operation is a mechanism where data representation is updated by running local filters or computations. Every node in the graph receives input only from its immediate neighbors.

C187.name: Aggregate function
C187.definition: Aggregate function is a mechanism used to combine information from a node's neighbors into a single representation. This function must be permutation-invariant, meaning the order in which the neighbor information is processed does not affect the final result.

C188.name: Update function
C188.definition: Update function is a process that modifies a node's vector representation. It combines the information received from neighbors (messages) with the node's existing self-knowledge to refine its representation.

C189.name: Multiset function
C189.definition: Multiset function is the technical name for a function that takes a set of items, which may contain duplicates, and maps them to a vector. This concept is used when the input node vectors might not be unique.

C190.name: Readout
C190.definition: Readout is the final step in a graph network that converts the set of individual node embeddings into a single vector embedding for the entire graph. This process is essentially another multiset function applied over all nodes.

C191.name: Message passing
C191.definition: Message passing is the process of unrolling message passing iterations where every step updates a set of node vectors by taking input data and combining information from neighboring nodes. This process is the forward pass through the network.

C192.name: Aggregate
C192.definition: Aggregate is the function that takes all node vectors from a node's neighbors and combines them into a single D-dimensional vector. This combined vector serves as the message passed to the central node.

C193.name: Update
C193.definition: Update is the function that takes a node's current node embedding plus the message received from its neighbors to provide an updated representation of that node. This function provides the new embedding for the node.

C194.name: Aggregation operation
C194.definition: Aggregation operation is a method of combining messages from neighbors that is not limited to simple summing or averaging. Instead, it is called attention, which is a summation dependent on the value of the node embeddings.

C195.name: Weight sharing idea
C195.definition: Weight sharing idea means that all the aggregate functions used in parallel across all operations within one layer of the message-passing algorithm are the same function. This allows the model to generalize across graphs of different sizes.

C196.name: Equivalence class
C196.definition: Equivalence class is a set of graphs that a graph net cannot distinguish from one another. If two graphs belong to the same equivalence class, the graph net must assign the same prediction to both.

C197.name: Tree structure
C197.definition: Tree structure is the local neighborhood pattern that a node observes when updating its representation based on incoming messages. This structure forms the entire characterization of the graph from the perspective of a graph net.

C198.name: Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm
C198.definition: Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm is a classical graph theory algorithm that takes two graphs and decides whether they are structurally the same or different. The power of a graph net to distinguish graphs is limited by the capabilities of this algorithm.

C199.name: Empirical risk
C199.definition: Empirical risk is the average loss incurred over all of the available training data points. This measure quantifies how well a model fits the specific data it was trained on.

C200.name: Population risk
C200.definition: Population risk is the expected error when making predictions on new samples drawn from the entire data generating process. This represents how well the model performs in the real world.

C201.name: Empirical test risk
C201.definition: Empirical test risk is the error measured specifically over a finite sample, such as a designated test set. This provides a practical estimate of the model's performance on unseen data.

C202.name: Generalization error
C202.definition: Generalization error is the difference between the empirical risk and the population risk. It measures how well a model performs on data outside of the training set.

C203.name: Memorization
C203.definition: Memorization is the process where a model simply stores and retrieves the exact answers from its training data. This behavior is characteristic of models like the filing cabinet, which do not learn underlying patterns.

C204.name: Data distribution
C204.definition: Data distribution is the underlying statistical pattern of the data that the model is trained on. Understanding this distribution is critical because if the training set does not represent all the interesting aspects of variation, generalization will fail.

C205.name: Filing cabinet
C205.definition: Filing cabinet is a simple model type that memorizes training data by predicting specific values only for the points it has seen. For all other points, the filing cabinet predicts zero.

C206.name: Large Language Model
C206.definition: Large Language Model (LLM) is a family of advanced deep nets, such as ChatGPT, that are capable of complex prediction tasks. These models are used to process sequences of words as input and generate predictions.

C207.name: Out-of-distribution input
C207.definition: Out-of-distribution input refers to data that is systematically different from the data the model was trained on. These inputs are outside the scope of the training population.

C208.name: Edge detector
C208.definition: Edge detector is a tool, specifically HED, used in the project as a proxy for what a human might have drawn. It is used instead of expensive human-hand-drawn sketches.

C209.name: Compositionality
C209.definition: Compositionality is a property where a system can take a new composition of things and factor them into independent components, such as patches. This allows the system to know what to do because it only needs to imitate the training data on those individual components.

C210.name: Occam's razor
C210.definition: Occam's razor is a principle stating that among competing explanations that fit the data equally well, one should prefer the simplest model. This principle suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.

C211.name: Generalization theory
C211.definition: Generalization theory is the study of how well a model trained on a specific dataset will perform when applied to unseen data. This theory is based on variations of Occam's razor.

C212.name: Heuristic
C212.definition: A heuristic is a practical approach or rule of thumb that is not rigorously proven but is used to guide decision-making. The initial statement regarding Occam's razor is considered a heuristic because measuring 'simplest' and 'generalization' requires mathematical precision.

C213.name: Shortest program
C213.definition: The shortest program is a concept from algorithmic information theory that serves as a rigorous version of Occam's razor. This program is the one that perfectly fits or generates the data and is predicted to generalize best.

C214.name: Bias
C214.definition: Bias is the training error, which represents the error incurred when the model is trained on the data. It is one component used in the bias-variance trade-off.

C215.name: Variance
C215.definition: Variance is the difference between the test error and the training error. It measures how much the model's predictions change when trained on different subsets of the data.

C216.name: Double descent
C216.definition: Double descent is a phenomenon where the generalization error of a model starts to improve again after initially worsening as the number of parameters increases. This suggests that the classical picture of overfitting is inaccurate.

C217.name: Model capacity
C217.definition: Model capacity is the complexity of a hypothesis space, which can be measured by the number of parameters. Controlling this capacity is necessary to prevent a model from overfitting.

C218.name: Interpolation threshold
C218.definition: Interpolation threshold is the point in model training where the model is capable of perfectly memorizing all the training data. This threshold marks the transition point where the model begins to fit the training data perfectly.

C219.name: VC dimension
C219.definition: VC dimension is a measure of capacity that counts the number of unique dichotomies a function class can apply to the training data. A higher VC dimension means the model can classify the training data in more different ways.

C220.name: Dichotomy
C220.definition: Dichotomy is a binary labeling of all the training data points, assigning each point to either a positive or negative class. This labeling is represented as a vector of assignments to positive one or negative one.

C221.name: VC theory (Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory)
C221.definition: VC theory is a framework that relates the size of the training data to the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space. This theory provides a guarantee that population error matches training error if the data size is sufficiently large relative to the hypothesis space size.

C222.name: Version space
C222.definition: The version space is the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the given training data. In neural networks, this is the set of all parameter settings that achieve zero training error.

C223.name: Parameter function map
C223.definition: The parameter function map is the relationship that connects the parameters (weights and biases) of a model to the actual mathematical function that the model defines. This map is many-to-one, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function.

C224.name: Simplicity bias
C224.definition: Simplicity bias is the tendency for deep nets to favor simple or smooth solutions when multiple solutions perfectly fit the training data. This bias suggests that the model naturally gravitates toward less complex functions.

C225.name: Lempel-Ziv complexity
C225.definition: Lempel-Ziv complexity is a specific measure of function complexity used to quantify how compressible a function's output is. It relates to how well a function's output can be compressed using a compression algorithm.

C226.name: Kernel matrix
C226.definition: Kernel matrix is a matrix that characterizes the representation of input data at the output of a neural network. Every row and column in this matrix represents a data point, and the value indicates the similarity between those two data points in the network's representational vectors.

C227.name: Rank
C227.definition: Rank is a measure of a matrix indicating the number of linearly independent rows and columns it contains. Blockier matrices, which indicate clustered data, tend to have a lower rank, suggesting a simpler data format.

C228.name: Effective rank
C228.definition: Effective rank is a variation of the matrix rank used to characterize the representation of data. Lower effective rank signifies a more clustered-like structure in the data representation.

C229.name: Weight decay
C229.definition: Weight decay is a type of explicit regularizer used in optimization. It works by tending to shrink the weights during each update step, which helps the network learn simpler solutions.

C230.name: Flat minima
C230.definition: Flat minima are basins in the objective function's energy landscape where the loss is low over a large region of the parameter space. These flat minima are argued to generalize better than narrow minima.

C231.name: Invariance
C231.definition: Invariance is a property where a model's output remains unchanged despite a transformation of the input, such as when a max pooling operation is applied over channels. This allows the model to be insensitive to specific input orientations.

C232.name: Equivariance
C232.definition: Equivariance is a property where a transformation applied to the input causes a corresponding, predictable transformation in the model's predictions. For instance, if the input nodes are permuted, the predictions will also be permuted.

C233.name: Domain knowledge
C233.definition: Domain knowledge is specialized information, such as equations of perspective projection or light transport, that is intentionally built into a neural architecture. This allows the model to generalize by using inherent structures rather than merely fitting the training data.

C234.name: Optimization
C234.definition: Optimization is the process of making the training of a deep learning model as efficient as possible. It is the primary focus area for improvement when the other puzzle pieces are addressed.

C235.name: Neural network
C235.definition: Neural network is a function that takes inputs and weights and produces an output. This function is the core component of the model being trained.

C236.name: Loss function
C236.definition: Loss function is the function used in optimization, and it can be replaced by a favorite norm when deriving different optimization algorithms.

C237.name: Learning rate
C237.definition: Learning rate is the step size, denoted as eta, which determines how large the steps are when moving the weights during the gradient descent operation.

C238.name: Stochastic gradients
C238.definition: Stochastic gradients are noisy estimates of the full gradient across all data points. These estimates are computed by calculating gradients only on a small handful of data points in each iteration.

C239.name: Scaling
C239.definition: Scaling refers to increasing the size of a neural network, which can be achieved by making the network wider or by making the network deeper. This process is done to improve the overall performance of the network.

C240.name: Training loss
C240.definition: Training loss is a metric that is plotted to show the performance of the network during the training process. It is used to observe how the network performs as its size or learning rate changes.

C241.name: Residual architecture
C241.definition: Residual architecture is a design technique used to fix scaling problems in deep networks. Using this architecture helps maintain performance even when the network is made deeper.

C242.name: Scaling the width
C242.definition: Scaling the width involves making the neural network wider, which is one method of increasing network size. This scaling generally leads to a better achieved loss, improving performance.

C243.name: First order methods
C243.definition: First order methods are optimization algorithms that rely exclusively on using the first derivatives of the loss function. These methods are the type of approach commonly used in deep learning.

C244.name: Second order methods
C244.definition: Second order methods are optimization algorithms that utilize both the first and the second derivatives of the loss function. These methods are distinguished by their use of second derivatives in addition to the first derivatives.

C245.name: Gradient
C245.definition: The gradient is the derivative of the loss with respect to the weights, which is the quantity obtained by performing back propagation. It is conceptually treated as one large vector.

C246.name: Hessian
C246.definition: The Hessian is a matrix of second derivatives that corresponds to all possible pairs of second derivatives. It is a matrix representation of the second derivatives of the loss function.

C247.name: Second derivative
C247.definition: The second derivative is a big matrix of second derivatives of the loss function with respect to the weights. This matrix is used by second order methods.

C248.name: Newton's method
C248.definition: Newton's method is an optimization algorithm that uses both first and second-order information to determine an optimization step. It is described as preconditioning the gradient with the inverse Hessian.

C249.name: Linearization of our loss function
C249.definition: Linearization of our loss function refers to the first-order term of the Taylor expansion. This term is defined as the gradient inner product delta w.

C250.name: Quadratic form
C250.definition: Quadratic form is the mathematical structure that the Taylor expansion takes when it is calculated up to the second order. This form is used when minimizing the loss function with respect to the weight perturbation delta w.

C251.name: Gauss-Newton decomposition
C251.definition: Gauss-Newton decomposition is a formula derived for the second derivative of a composite objective function. This decomposition splits the full Hessian into two pieces based on the product rule.

C252.name: Composite objective function
C252.definition: A composite objective function is a function that is the composition of two other functions. This structure is common in machine learning, such as when combining an error function and a neural network.

C253.name: Gauss-Newton method
C253.definition: The Gauss-Newton method is an algorithm derived from the Gauss-Newton decomposition. It provides an iterative weight update using a specific form of the Hessian.

C254.name: Squared error
C254.definition: Squared error is a specific error measure that is often assumed in the context of the Gauss-Newton method. For this measure, the second derivative with respect to the model is simplified to a constant value.

C255.name: Low rank Gaussian approximation
C255.definition: Low rank Gaussian approximation is a mathematical assumption where the approximation used in the model has a low rank. This condition can be a reason why certain optimization methods might be desirable.

C256.name: Forward mode automatic differentiation
C256.definition: Forward mode automatic differentiation is a technique used for calculating derivatives, which is noted to be significantly more computationally expensive than backpropagation.

C257.name: Extra derivatives
C257.definition: Extra derivatives are additional derivatives that must be computed when using certain optimization methods, beyond the standard regular gradient. These computations, along with matrix inversion, are practical drawbacks of certain methods.

C258.name: Steepest descent
C258.definition: Steepest descent is an optimization algorithm that decomposes the movement into a step size and a step direction. The direction chosen determines how the algorithm moves toward minimizing the loss function.

C259.name: Infinity norm
C259.definition: The infinity norm is a measure that determines the maximum size of a vector across all its coordinates. When using this norm, the unit ball takes on the shape of a square.

C260.name: Singular Value Decomposition
C260.definition: Singular Value Decomposition is a generalized eigenvalue decomposition that every matrix possesses. This decomposition allows one to mentally break down each weight matrix in a neural network.

C261.name: Frobenius norm
C261.definition: Frobenius norm is one specific example of a matrix norm used to measure the size of a neural network's weight matrices.

C262.name: Dual norm
C262.definition: Dual norm is a concept that every norm has, and it appears in the general formulation of the solution to the steepest descent problem.

C263.name: Steepest descent problem
C263.definition: Steepest descent problem is an optimization problem whose solution can be separated into two distinct parts: computing the step size and computing the direction.

C264.name: Non-isotropic space
C264.definition: Non-isotropic space is a mathematical space where the axes are not equal to each other, meaning that different directions have different scales or magnitudes. This condition arises when the loss function does not have the property that all directions in the weight space are equal.

C265.name: Preconditioner matrix
C265.definition: Preconditioner matrix is a tool used to scale each coordinate in the weight space at a different rate. This scaling allows the optimization process to account for the non-uniform nature of the space.

C266.name: Matrix norm
C266.definition: Matrix norm is a mathematical tool used to measure the size or scale of a matrix. It allows researchers to quantify whether a weight update is too big or too small.

C267.name: Spectral norm
C267.definition: Spectral norm is a type of matrix norm defined as the largest singular value of a matrix.

C268.name: Nuclear norm
C268.definition: Nuclear norm is one of the specific types of matrix norms available for measuring the size of a matrix.

C269.name: Schatten p-norms
C269.definition: Schatten p-norms represent a general class of norms that can be used to measure the size of a matrix.

C270.name: Induced operator norm
C270.definition: Induced operator norm is a way to define a norm on a matrix based on specific norms chosen for the input and output spaces. This definition is achieved by specifying a norm on the input space and a norm on the output space.

C271.name: RMS to RMS operator norm
C271.definition: RMS to RMS operator norm is a specific norm used to initialize and update weight matrices such that the norm of the matrix or update is around 1. This normalization helps control RMS norms as data moves through the network.

C272.name: Operator norm
C272.definition: Operator norm is a mathematical measure that provides an upper-bound on how much the features of a particular layer can change. This norm does not guarantee that the features will change by this amount, only that they cannot change more than this amount.

C273.name: Width scaling problem
C273.definition: Width scaling problem is the issue that defining a particular norm helps to solve, specifically related to maintaining stable training when varying the width of a neural network.

C274.name: Expressivity
C274.definition: Expressivity is the capacity of the neural network to approximate functions, and the goal is to constrain network properties without damaging this approximation capacity.

C275.name: Well-scaled depth limit
C275.definition: Well-scaled depth limit is a condition where a compound system, composed of many terms, remains stable when the number of terms approaches infinity. This stability is achieved by carefully scaling the internals of the system.

C276.name: Residual network
C276.definition: Residual network is an architecture where a single block takes an input $x$ and returns $x$ plus the block's output of $x$. This structure allows for the composition of many blocks while maintaining a nice function.

C277.name: Block multiplier
C277.definition: Block multiplier is a factor placed in front of blocks within a residual network. This factor is crucial for ensuring that the network's dynamics do not blow up or go to zero as the depth increases.

C278.name: Module
C278.definition: A module is an abstraction that handles inputs in an input space, outputs in an output space, and possesses weights in a weight space. Modules can represent either an individual layer or a full neural network.

C279.name: Atomic module
C279.definition: An atomic module is one of the basic layer types that forms the library, such as ReLU, linear, convolution, or embedding. These modules are the fundamental building blocks of the network.

C280.name: Forward function
C280.definition: A forward function is the function that the module expresses, which represents the primary operation of the module. This function dictates how the module processes its inputs.

C281.name: Backward function
C281.definition: A backward function is the derivatives of the forward function. This function is necessary for computing the derivatives during optimization.

C282.name: Transformer
C282.definition: Transformer is a neural network architecture that utilizes the attention mechanism, allowing it to process input data by dynamically determining the weights for linear combinations.

C283.name: Attention
C283.definition: Attention is the key concept that is genuinely new to the field, while other components of the transformer are merely new names for existing ideas.

C284.name: Token
C284.definition: Token is a vector of numbers that represents a descriptive part of the input data, such as a patch of an image or a word.

C285.name: Locality bias
C285.definition: Locality bias is the inherent characteristic of CNNs that forces them to factorize the signal processing problem into small, local pieces.

C286.name: Fully connected network
C286.definition: Fully connected network is a type of neural network where every single output neuron is connected to every input neuron. This structure allows information to be aggregated immediately and globally across the entire input.

C287.name: Sparsely globally
C287.definition: Sparsely globally is an approach that allows a network to look at the entire input signal without requiring every neuron to be connected to every other neuron. This method maintains a global view while significantly reducing the computational load and number of parameters.

C288.name: Set of tokens
C288.definition: Set of tokens is the primary data structure used to represent information in the transformer model. This set consists of multiple tokens, which are the basic units over which the transformer operates.

C289.name: Tokenization
C289.definition: Tokenization is the general strategy where a domain expert converts raw data into discrete tokens that the generic transformer can process. Tokenization allows the transformer to operate on chunks of data that make sense within the specific domain.

C290.name: Byte pair
C290.definition: Byte pair is a specific unit used in natural language processing that represents two byte representations of the language. Byte pair allows the system to carve up English and other natural language into manageable units.

C291.name: Linear combination operation
C291.definition: Linear combination operation is a generalization of the linear combination that is performed over neurons. This operation is one of the two basic operations used when operating over tokens.

C292.name: Linear combination of tokens
C292.definition: Linear combination of tokens is a weighted combination of vectors, where the vectors represent the tokens. This operation is represented in matrix notation by multiplying a weight matrix by the token matrix.

C293.name: Low rank transformation
C293.definition: Low rank transformation is a mathematical operation where the number of weights determining the combination is significantly smaller than the total number of individual neurons that make up the tokens. This makes the token linear combination a less expressive family of layers.

C294.name: Token-wise nonlinearity
C294.definition: Token-wise nonlinearity is a function that operates on each token independently and identically. This nonlinearity passes every token in the array through the same nonlinear function F.

C295.name: Token net
C295.definition: Token net is an architecture that performs a linear combination of tokens. This process involves taking a weighted sum of tokens, followed by a token-wise nonlinearity.

C296.name: Linear combination
C296.definition: Linear combination is a mathematical operation where the output is calculated as a weighted sum of input tokens, which is the basis for how tokens are combined into a new representation.

C297.name: Unrolled GNN (Graph Neural Network)
C297.definition: Unrolled GNN is a network structure that utilizes an aggregate function for weighted combination and often shares weights across its depth. This structure is equivalent to the token net version of the transformer.

C298.name: Weight matrix
C298.definition: Weight matrix is a matrix containing free parameters that determines the coefficients used in a linear combination, which can either be learned via backpropagation or determined by external activations.

C299.name: Query
C299.definition: Query is a special operation that emits a vector based on the contents of the question's embedding vector. This vector is used to determine which parts of the input signal the model should attend to.

C300.name: Query-key-value attention
C300.definition: Query-key-value attention is the mathematical formulation of the most common kind of attention, which allows the transformer to map from a set of input tokens to a set of output tokens. This mechanism involves using a query to determine relevance against keys and then aggregating values.

C301.name: Key
C301.definition: Key is a function associated with each token that emits a vector, which the query attempts to match against. This vector represents the content of the token that the query should match to.

C302.name: Value
C302.definition: Value is an operation that transforms a token vector into the information that will be reported to the next layer of the network. This vector contains the actual content that is retrieved when a query matches a key.

C303.name: Dot product
C303.definition: Dot product between the key vector and the query vector measures how relevant a specific key is to a specific query. This operation functions as a way of measuring the similarity between the two vectors.

C304.name: Attention layer
C304.definition: Attention layer is a concrete mechanism that utilizes three learnable matrices to transform a token vector into query, key, and value vectors. These projections constitute the learnable parameters of the attention layer.

C305.name: Learnable parameters
C305.definition: Learnable parameters are the matrices that the model learns during training, such as the matrices that transform a token vector into a query, key, or value. These parameters are essential components of the attention layer.

C306.name: Query vector
C306.definition: Query vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to determine the relevance of other tokens. The query function maps from the question vector, which is represented by a token vector.

C307.name: Key vector
C307.definition: Key vector is a linear projection of the token vector, which is used to be compared against a query vector. This comparison measures the similarity between the key and the query.

C308.name: Self-attention
C308.definition: Self-attention is an idea where the weights used in a linear combination are determined as a function of the input sequence itself. This allows the model to weigh the importance of different tokens relative to each other.

C309.name: Value vector
C309.definition: Value vector is a vector emitted by every token in the input sequence via a projection (WV) that holds the actual information being combined in the linear combination. The attention mechanism weights these vectors to form the output.

C310.name: Attention equation
C310.definition: Attention equation is the mathematical condensation of the self-attention process, which involves multiplying the query matrix by the transpose of the key matrix. This operation calculates the similarity between all pairs of queries and keys.

C311.name: Convolution
C311.definition: Convolution is a computational operation that uses a much lower rank matrix compared to a fully connected layer. This structure allows for far fewer learnable parameters while maintaining translation equivariance.

C312.name: Low rank
C312.definition: Low rank describes a matrix that can be represented using fewer parameters than its full dimensions would suggest. This property is advantageous because it reduces the number of linear learnable parameters in the model.

C313.name: Set-to-set mapping
C313.definition: Set-to-set mapping is a function where an unordered set of inputs maps to an unordered set of outputs. This characteristic implies that the ordering of the tokens does not inherently matter for the transformation.

C314.name: Autoregressive model
C314.definition: Autoregressive model predicts the next word in a sequence by taking the previous prediction and appending it to the input sequence, then continuing the process. This model is trained to ensure its predictions match the actual text observed in the training set.

C315.name: Causal attention
C315.definition: Causal attention is an extra piece that is important when mapping transformers onto language models. This mechanism is necessary for the model to process information sequentially.

C316.name: Autoregressive transformer
C316.definition: Autoregressive transformer is a type of transformer that generates output sequentially by predicting the next item in a sequence based on previously generated items. The process involves predicting the next item, shifting the input, and repeating the cycle.

C317.name: Causal masking
C317.definition: Causal masking is a technique applied to the attention matrix that ensures every output token can only attend to tokens that appeared earlier in the sequence. This operation prevents the model from looking into the future, which is necessary for generating text in time's order.

C318.name: Transformer architecture
C318.definition: Transformer architecture is a model defined by the paper "Attention Is All You Need" that utilizes attention mechanisms as its primary component for processing sequences.

C319.name: Feedforward
C319.definition: Feedforward is the token-wise nonlinearity that involves applying a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) independently and identically to every single token vector.

C320.name: Autoregressive part
C320.definition: Autoregressive part is a component of the model related to autoregressive modeling, where the prediction process generates outputs sequentially based on previous steps.

C321.name: Cross-attention
C321.definition: Cross-attention is a mechanism where a set of tokens attends to a different, separate set of tokens, such as text tokens attending to image tokens.

C322.name: Hacks
C322.definition: Hacks are practical tips and methods that have historically driven progress in deep learning. These are often anecdotal insights from practitioners rather than formal mathematical theory.

C323.name: VC dimension (Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension)
C323.definition: VC dimension is a classical theoretical measure used to establish generalization bounds. These bounds predict how well a system will perform based on its complexity.

C324.name: Generalization bounds
C324.definition: Generalization bounds are theoretical limits derived from classical theories that predict how well a system will perform. These bounds can be rendered vacuous when dealing with deep nets.

C325.name: Pixel
C325.definition: Pixel is the fundamental unit of data, particularly in image analysis, which requires deep inspection rather than relying solely on summary statistics. Becoming friends with every pixel means thoroughly examining the raw data points in a domain.

C326.name: Spurious correlation
C326.definition: Spurious correlation is a shortcut where a deep net uses an irrelevant feature, such as a marker in the corner of an image, instead of the actual tissue to make a classification.

C327.name: Bias in the data
